title: Lage utrop med for og så — exclamations
goal: Choose noun-focused for or degree-focused så without question inversion.

objectives.statement: Choose noun-focused for or degree-focused så without question inversion.

spans.value: Maja and Elias have rented a cabin by a fjord. They arrive late in the afternoon and walk through the rooms for the first time.
For et hyggelig sted!
Ja, og så stille det er her!

blocks.translation: Yes, and how quiet it is here!

spans.value: Se på fjorden. For en utsikt!

blocks.translation: Look at the fjord. What a view!

spans.value: Så blå himmelen er i dag!

blocks.translation: How blue the sky is today!

spans.value: Og for noen store vinduer huset har!

blocks.translation: And what large windows the house has!

spans.value: Ja, så lyst det er inne!

blocks.translation: Yes, how bright it is inside!

spans.value: Maja and Elias are not asking for information. They are reacting emotionally to what they see. Norwegian commonly uses
for
or
så
for this kind of exclamation, but the two words focus attention differently:

items.value: when the exclamation focuses on a person, thing, place, or other noun.
when it focuses on how strong a quality is.

spans.value: Compare Maja’s and Elias’s reactions to the same view:
The first reaction presents the view as an impressive thing. The second emphasizes the degree of its beauty.
Use
for
before a noun phrase when your reaction is mainly about the person or thing itself. A common pattern is:
The article agrees with the noun in the usual way:
The adjective is useful but not always necessary:
These short exclamations do not need a verb. The situation makes the reaction clear.
A longer
for
exclamation can include a full statement:

no.value: For en fin leilighet dere har!

en.value: What a nice apartment you have!

no.value: For et godt måltid du har laget!

en.value: What a good meal you have made!

no.value: For noen interessante historier hun forteller!

spans.value: Notice the statement word order in the final part:
The subject comes before the verb. Although the sentence expresses surprise or admiration, it is not a question.
Use
så
when the main point is how beautiful, cold, fast, quiet, expensive, or otherwise striking something is. In this use,
så
strengthens an adjective or adverb.
A short reaction can end immediately after the description:
When the person or thing being described is named, a common pattern is:
The focus falls on the strength or degree of the description: the apartment is remarkably nice, the kitchen remarkably large, and the runner remarkably fast.

sections.title: The contrast at the heart of the lesson

spans.value: This is the contrast at the heart of the lesson:
The
for
sentence packages the reaction around a noun:
evening, mountain, runners, song
. The
så
sentence highlights the quality or manner:
peaceful, high, fast, beautifully
English exclamations beginning with
how
can make Norwegian learners expect question-like word order. Norwegian
så
exclamations do not use question inversion.
A normal statement has the subject before the verb:
The corresponding exclamation keeps the subject before the verb:
Do not move the verb in front of the subject:
With that word order and question intonation, the sentence is interpreted as a question rather than the intended exclamation.
Compare:
And:
The compact rule is:

statement.value: exclamation, place the description first, then keep the subject before the verb.

spans.value: This also applies when the subject is a pronoun:
Longer
for
exclamations follow the same principle:

no.value: For en hyggelig nabo vi har!

en.value: What a nice neighbor we have!

spans.value: The ending is
vi har
, not question order.
A common mistake is to begin with
så
and then continue with the noun pattern used after
for
Intended meaning:
What a beautiful view!
Use either the noun-focused pattern:
Or the degree-focused pattern:
Another mistake is to omit the article after
for
when a singular countable noun needs one:
Intended meaning:
What a beautiful view!

blocks.translation: Yes, and how clearly we could see the stars!

spans.value: Fint! Dere hadde vel ikke problemer med peisen?

blocks.translation: Good! You didn’t have any problems with the fireplace, did you?

spans.value: Nei. Så lett den var å bruke!

blocks.translation: No. How easy it was to use!

spans.value: Og for en god frokost vi spiste på terrassen!

blocks.translation: And what a good breakfast we ate on the terrace!

prompt.value: Ingrid writes: «Hytta har store vinduer. Fjorden er svært vakker, og det er helt stille om kvelden.» Reply to Ingrid in a message. Thank her for the stay and comment on at least two details, using one exclamation that begins with «for» and one that begins with «så».

explanation.value: Svaret takker Ingrid for hytta eller oppholdet, kommenterer minst to detaljer og bruker begge utropsmønstrene.

payload.judge_prompt: Check the response against all gating criteria. Any full clause used for an exclamation must keep statement word order, with the subject before the verb; question inversion fails the word-order criterion. Do not require a full clause when an otherwise valid exclamation does not use one.

criteria.instruction: The Norwegian message is addressed or clearly directed to Ingrid.
The message thanks Ingrid for the cabin or the stay.
The message reacts to at least two supplied details: the large windows, the beautiful fjord, or the quiet evenings.
The message contains a noun-focused exclamation built with «for en/et/noen ...».
The message contains a degree-focused exclamation built with «så» followed by an adjective or adverb.
Any full clause used for an exclamation keeps statement word order, with the subject before the verb; question inversion fails this criterion. A full clause is not required.
